info.title: IQM Server API
info.description:
> [!CAUTION]
>  Please note that this IQM Server API is currently in development and may be subject to changes. For reference,
our legacy API documentation can be found [here](?api=integration). However, we advise against integrating with the legacy version,
as it will be deprecated soon. Additionally, access to the legacy integration API now requires IP whitelisting by IQM Resonance.


The **IQM Server API** is an HTTP interface that provides programmatic access to IQM Quantum Computer resources.
It is used by the official IQM client tools, but external parties can also use it for custom integrations.

The IQM Server API replaces the following legacy APIs:

- Station API (On-Prem only)
- Resonance API (Cloud only)
- Cocos API (On-Prem and Cloud)

This API focuses on job submission and execution. Management and maintenance
operations — such as user, organization, and team management — are provided by
the separate [GraphQL API](/docs/graphql-api-reference).

## API Versioning

The API follows this versioning scheme:

```plain
/api/<version>/<resource>
```

The latest API version can be accessed using the alias `latest`:

```plain
/api/latest/<resource>
```

Available versions can be queried with:

```plain
GET /api/versions
```

#### Major changes (breaking)

When a breaking change is introduced, a new API version is published, and the old one remains available
for existing clients. Clients are strongly encouraged to pin to a fixed version for stability. The `latest`
alias should only be used for development and testing.

#### Minor changes (non-breaking)

IQM Server may introduce backwards-compatible changes to existing versions. Clients are expected to handle
these gracefully.

Data Sent by the Server

- JSON objects: new properties may be added to existing schemas. Clients must ignore unknown properties
  (implicit `"additionalProperties": true`).
- Protobuf messages: new fields may be added. Clients must ignore unknown fields, as described in the
  [Protobuf language guide](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/proto3/#updating).
- Schema narrowing: for example, if a schema was `error_code: int | string`, it may later be restricted
  to `error_code: int` without affecting runtime behavior.
- Enums and `one_of` fields: variants may be removed as long as runtime behavior is preserved.

Data Sent by the Client

- JSON objects: Clients must not send extra properties. Although the server may ignore them, new optional
  input properties added in the future could conflict and cause requests to fail.
- Protobuf messages: Clients must not send unknown fields for the same reason.

#### Endpoints

The list of endpoints is not guaranteed to be static. New endpoints may be added to existing versions.

### Deprecation

When a new version is released, older versions are automatically marked as deprecated.
If a client uses a deprecated version, the server will include this response header:

```
IQM-API-Deprecated: true
```

Deprecated versions may be removed after a deprecation period, so clients should migrate promptly.

The server may also mark individual operations as deprecated. In this case, responses will include:

```
IQM-API-Operation-Deprecated: true; breaking=<version>
```

Where `<version>` is the API version in which the operation will stop working. If this header is absent,
upgrading to a newer version should not break the operation.

## Authentication

All requests to the IQM Server API require an API Token. The token must be passed as a Bearer token in
the `Authorization` header:

```
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" https://<server-url>/api/<version>/<resource>
```

API tokens are available from the server web dashboard under the profile menu. They are personal and scoped
to a single workspace. If a user has multiple workspaces, each requires its own token.

### Token scopes

Each token is assigned one or more scopes when created. Scopes limit what the token can do: a token's effective permissions are the intersection of its owner's role permissions and its assigned scopes, plus a small set of baseline operations always available regardless of scopes. Always choose the narrowest scopes needed to limit exposure if the token is ever leaked.
You can check the scopes of existing tokens in your user profile view and in the [List API tokens](#tag/token-management/get/api/v1/tokens) endpoint.

The available scopes are:

- `job_execution` — submit and manage your own jobs, list timeslots in the current account.
  This covers all usage of the iqm-client python library.
- `timeslot_management` — view and book or cancel timeslots.
- `account_management` — manage workspace members and teams, and transfer credits between workspaces.
- `account_analytics` — read-only access to workspace members' job metadata, analytics, and credits history.

For this REST API, the only relevant scopes are Job Execution and Timeslot Management. The other two scopes are needed for certain operations in the [GraphQL API](/docs/graphql-api-reference).

A token with no scopes can reach only operations without any scope requirements.

## Rate limiting

The IQM Server API is rate-limited per user account. The rate limit is _quota-based_ —
each user has their own quota of (opaque) cost units and each request consumes a small
budget from this quota. The cost per request is endpoint-specific and described in
the endpoint documentation. When the quota is exceeded, subsequent requests are blocked
with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests`. The quota resets over a short rolling window.

The rate limit quotas, time window duration and API endpoint request costs might be adjusted without
prior notice, so clients are expected to follow their quota usage from the response headers
(see below) and to obey the `Retry-After` timeouts for the best operational reliability.

The currently applied values are:

- User-specific quota: **3000 units**
- Rate-limit window duration: **10 seconds**
- Block duration: **30 seconds**

### Response headers

The current quota usage can be followed per request using the
[IETF rate limit headers](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-polli-ratelimit-headers-02.html).
Successful responses carry the following headers:

```
RateLimit-Limit: <units>
RateLimit-Remaining: <units>
```

Clients should monitor `RateLimit-Remaining` and slow down before it reaches zero, rather
than trying to derive an absolute request rate from these values.

When the quota is exceeded, subsequent requests are rejected with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests`
until the block expires. The response carries:

```
Retry-After: <seconds>
```

Clients must wait at least the indicated number of seconds before retrying. The `RateLimit-*`
headers are not included on `429` responses. The response body uses the standard JSON error
shape; see the `RateLimitExceeded` schema.

get.description:
Retrieves the job status and state metadata of a job identified by its job ID.

Note that this response does not include raw job artifact data (e.g., measurement
results). To access artifact data, use the **Get job artifact** endpoint once the
artifacts become available for the job.

When `wait_until_terminal=true` is supplied the server holds the request open
for up to `timeout_seconds` seconds (default 10, max 30) while it waits for the
job to reach a terminal API status (one of `completed`, `failed`, or
`cancelled`). If the timeout elapses first, the server responds with the
current job state and sets the `IQM-Long-Poll-Timed-Out: true` response header
so clients can reissue the request without parsing the body.


Rate-limit request cost: **10**

parameters.name: wait_until_terminal
parameters.description:
When `true`, the server holds the request open until the job reaches a
terminal API status — one of `completed`, `failed`, or `cancelled` — or
the timeout elapses. If the job is already terminal the server responds
immediately. When omitted or `false` the endpoint returns the current
job state without waiting.

parameters.name: timeout_seconds
parameters.description:
Maximum number of seconds the server will hold the request open when
`wait_until_terminal=true`. Must be between 0 and 30 (inclusive).
Defaults to 10. Ignored when `wait_until_terminal` is not set. When the
timeout elapses before the job reaches a terminal API status, the
server returns the current job state and sets the
`IQM-Long-Poll-Timed-Out: true` response header.

IQM-Long-Poll-Timed-Out.description: Set to `true` when `wait_until_terminal=true` was requested and the configured timeout elapsed before the job reached a terminal status. Omitted otherwise.

get.description:
Retrieves the original input payload of a job identified by its job ID.

The payload is returned exactly as it was at the time of submission,
without any modifications. If the job type’s payload schema changes in
the future, those changes are not applied to previously submitted job payloads.

The type of the submitted job is provided in the `IQM-Job-Type` response header.

Payloads are stored in a compressed format. For best performance, include
`Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate` in the request headers so that IQM Server can
serve the stored data directly.


Rate-limit request cost: **10**

get.description:
Returns the current status of the pay-as-you-go queue for this quantum computer.
Indicates the number of jobs currently queued as well as the time slots
during which the queued jobs are executed. The availability windows
are only accurate at the time of the request. Future user bookings
will affect execution of the pay-as-you-go queue.

The start and end time of returned availability windows are always truncated to the
`timerange_start` and `timerange_end` provided in the request.

This endpoint can be accessed with regular workspace tokens and with system administration tokens.


Rate-limit request cost: **10**

parameters.name: timerange_start
parameters.description:
Start of the time range to query.
Must be a UTC timestamp in RFC3339 format with 'Z' time zone indicator.
Defaults to now if not provided.

parameters.name: timerange_end
parameters.description:
End of the time range to check for availability of the pay-as-you-go queue.
Must be a UTC timestamp in RFC3339 format with 'Z' time zone indicator.

post.description:
Books one or more timeslots on a given quantum computer. The slot references should match values returned by the timeslot listing endpoint (`GET`). If `expected_price` is provided for a slot, the request will fail when the current price differs from the expected value. All slots are booked atomically — if any slot fails, none are booked. Credits are charged immediately upon successful booking.

**Note:** Only users with the "scheduler" or "admin" role in an organization or team can book timeslots.

delete.description:
Cancels one or more previously booked timeslots and refunds the credits that
were charged at booking time. Cancellation is only possible before the
`cancellation_deadline` time set on the timeslot (typically 48 hours before the
slot start). The timeslot references must match values returned by the timeslot
listing or booking endpoint. All cancellations are performed atomically — if
any timeslot fails, none are cancelled.

Malformed timeslot references are rejected at input validation with a `400 Bad
Request` before any cancellation is attempted.
For all other failures, the response is `403 Forbidden` with error details
identifying which references prevented cancellation. Possible per-reference
issue codes:

- `qc_mismatch`: the timeslot reference does not belong to the quantum
  computer specified in the path.
- `not_found`: no timeslot with this reference exists for the current user.
- `deadline_passed`: the cancellation deadline for this timeslot has already
  passed.


Rate-limit request cost: **100**

post.description:
> [!note]
> This endpoint is only relevant to refreshable tokens.

This endpoint activates a token previously created with the "refresh" endpoint.
It is only useful for tokens created with the property `"activated": false` in the refresh request.
It is idempotent and has no effect on already activated tokens.

Once the token is activated, the refresh token used to create it becomes invalid.

This endpoint enforces the active token limit. The request will fail with 403
if the user already has the maximum number of active tokens.

## Authentication

This endpoint requires that the `Authorization` header bearer token
is the same **refresh token** that was used to create the API token.


Rate-limit request cost: **100**

post.description:
> [!note]
> This endpoint is only relevant to refreshable tokens.

This endpoint creates a new API token based on a refresh token associated with an existing API token.

If the property `"activated"` is set to `true` or omitted entirely,
the created token is activated immediately and the refresh token used to create it
is invalidated right away.

### Two-phase activation

Because networking is unreliable, an HTTP response might fail during the refresh operation, invalidating the refresh token forever. To prevent the loss of tokens, we support
[two-phase commit protocol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-phase_commit_protocol) for the refresh
operation.

If the property `"activated": false` is set in the request body, the created token needs
to be activated using the `/tokens/current/activate` endpoint before it can be used.
The used refresh token remains valid until the new token is activated.

This avoids invalidating the refresh token before the user receives it successfully.

## Token limit

If `"activated": true` (or omitted), this endpoint enforces the active token limit.
The request will fail with 403 if the user already has the maximum number of active tokens.

## Authentication

This endpoint requires that the `Authorization` header bearer token
is an active **refresh token**.


Rate-limit request cost: **100**

Revokes the API token and its associated refresh token.
Once revoked, the tokens can no longer be used for authentication.

This endpoint is idempotent and has no effect on already revoked tokens.

# Authentication
This endpoint may be invoked with the regular authentication methods
available in this API. It does not accept refresh tokens for authentication.

iqm.server.Job.description: Representation of a single submitted quantum job.

id.description: Job id, stable during the whole lifetime of the job.

qc.description: The quantum computer to which the job was submitted.

status.description:
The current status of the job. This will change when the job
is being processed by the system. See `JobStatus` for the
possible statuses.

queue_position.description: Job's position in the queue (if applicable)

oneOf.description: Job's compilation state. Not present if the job hasn't been compiled yet
Job's execution state. Not present if the job hasn't been executed yet

runtime_ms.description:
Job runtime is a sum of compilation (if applicable, for Circuit jobs) and execution durations,
in milliseconds. Available for completed jobs.

Deprecated: use `metrics.runtime_seconds`.

metrics.description: Timing and billing metrics recorded for the job.

timeline.description: The timeline of events occurred to the job.

artifacts.description: List of the available artifacts for the job.

messages.description: Informational messages related to the job processing.

errors.description:
If the job is rejected or failed, errors leading to the
failure will be in this error list.

tag.description: Optional user-defined tag associated with the job.

dashboard_url.description: Link to this job in the dashboard UI.

iqm.server.JobArtifact.description: Representation of a single downloadable job artifact.

type.description:
The type of this artifact; artifact data can be loaded by type, see
`/jobs/{job_id}/artifacts/{artifact_type}` for more details.

execution_runtime_estimate_ms.description:
The estimated execution runtime of the compiled job, in milliseconds.

Deprecated: use `execution_runtime_estimate_seconds`.

execution_runtime_estimate_seconds.description: The estimated execution runtime of the compiled job, in seconds.

calibration_set_id.description:
The calibration set id that was used to compile the job.
Not applicable for pulse level jobs.

iqm.server.JobError.description: Representation of a job error that occurred during the processing.

error_code.description: Machine-readable reason code for the error

iqm.server.JobMessage.description: Representation of a job error that occurred during the processing.

iqm.server.JobMetrics.description:
Timing and billing metrics recorded for a job. Durations are null until the
quantum computer reports them, so they are typically available only for
finished jobs.

compilation_seconds.description: Time spent compiling the job on the quantum computer, in seconds.

execution_seconds.description: Time spent executing the job on the quantum computer, in seconds.

runtime_seconds.description: Total runtime in seconds: compilation plus execution.

billed_seconds.description:
Billed runtime in whole seconds: `runtime_seconds` rounded up. Credits
are charged on this value.

iqm.server.JobStatus.description:
List of possible job statuses
  * `waiting`:
        Job is in the queue waiting for validation or execution
  * `processing`:
        The job is being processed currently. To see the more detailed
        overall processing status, see `job.execution` and `job.compilation`.
  * `completed`:
        Job has been completed successfully.
  * `failed`:
        Job execution has failed. The failure reason is listed in the
        `job.errors` property.
  * `cancelled`:
        Job was cancelled by the user.

iqm.server.JobSweepProgress.description: Represents the ongoing progress of a parallel sweep.

max_value.description: Maximum number of iterations until the sweep resets.

value.description: Current iteration in the sweep, in range `[0, max_value]`.

iqm.server.JobTimelineEvent.description: Representation of a single job timeline event.

iqm.server.QcAdditionalInfo.description: Additional information and links for a quantum computer.

academy_url.description: Link to IQM Academy content relevant to this quantum computer.

best_suited_for.description: Free-form list of use cases this quantum computer is best suited for.

documentation_url.description: Link to documentation for this quantum computer.

mock_url.description: Link to a mock environment for this quantum computer.

iqm.server.QcHealthStatus.description: The current operational status and health of a quantum computer.

operational_status.description: Whether the quantum computer is online or under maintenance.

healthy.description: Whether the quantum computer is healthy.

updated_at.description: Time the health was last checked.

health.description:
Health readings. Present only when `operational_status` is `online` and a
health check has already run.

iqm.server.QcLimits.description: The job size limits of this Quantum Computer.

max_instructions_per_circuit.description:
Maximum number of instructions within any circuit, if applicable to the

tags.name: Quantum computers
tags.description:
The **Quantum Computers API** provides functionality for listing available
quantum computers along with their capabilities and configurations.

Different quantum computers may run different versions of Station Control,
which can result in variations in configuration and capability. This API
allows clients to programmatically retrieve the specific capabilities and
configurations for each quantum computer.

tags.name: Jobs
tags.description:
The **Jobs API** provides functionality for executing various types of quantum jobs on
available quantum computers.

## Job execution flow

When a job is submitted to the server, the server validates the schema of the job
payload. If the payload is valid, the job is placed in the execution queue. The server
supports two types of queues: a basic **on-demand (FIFO) queue** and a **timeslot**
queue. By default, jobs are submitted to the on-demand queue unless explicitly specified
otherwise by the client. A job remains in this queue until all preceding jobs have
been executed.

When it is time to execute a job, it is sent to the quantum computer’s **Station Control**
software, which compiles and runs the job. During this stage, the semantic contents of
the job (e.g., qubit names or gate locations) are validated against the quantum computer’s
topology. If the job is executable on that system, it is executed, and the results are
post-processed by Station Control. The processed results are then stored on the server,
where they are persisted and made available for client download.

## Job cancellation

Jobs can be cancelled at any time before they reach a terminal status. Once a job has
reached a terminal status, cancellation is no longer possible. If a job is in progress
when a cancellation occurs, the server interrupts its execution. In such cases, any artifacts
generated before the interruption remain available, but some post-processed artifacts (e.g.,
measurement counts) may be missing.

## Job queue types

### On-demand queue

The on-demand queue executes jobs in the order they arrive (FIFO). This is the default
queue type.

### Timeslot queue

If an account has a reserved timeslot, jobs can be submitted to the timeslot queue,
which executes jobs in FIFO order during the active timeslot. If the account does not
have any booked timeslots, submitting a job to the timeslot queue is not permitted.
If all queued jobs cannot be executed within the timeslot, they are returned to the
queue and wait for the next available timeslot.

The timeslot queue can be activated by including the parameter `use_timeslot=true`
when submitting the job.

## Job access control

Jobs are accessible only to the user who submitted them. Each job is also associated
with an account (personal, organizational, or team). Users must access jobs using the
same account that was used for submission.

This account association is derived implicitly from the API token used. API tokens
belong to a single account, and all API requests (including job submission and retrieval)
use that token for access control. If a user belongs to multiple accounts, care must be
taken to ensure that the correct API token is used at all times.

## Long-polling for job state

The **Get job** endpoint supports long-polling so clients can wait for a job
to reach a terminal status without repeatedly re-issuing the request. Pass
`wait_until_terminal=true` on the query string to enable it, optionally with
`timeout_seconds` (0–30 seconds, default 10) to cap how long the server will
hold the request open. Both parameters are optional; omitting them preserves
the original non-blocking behaviour.

- **Job reached a terminal status before the timeout:** the server responds
  as soon as the job is terminal and returns the current job state.
- **Timeout elapsed first:** the server responds with the current
  (non-terminal) job state and sets the `IQM-Long-Poll-Timed-Out: true`
  response header. The header is omitted when the job reached a terminal
  status before the timeout, so clients can use its mere presence as the
  timeout signal and reissue the request to keep waiting.

Authentication, authorization, and ownership semantics are identical to a
regular **Get job** request: requests against jobs that do not exist or are
owned by a different user return `404`.

## Job lifecycle and data retention

Job data (including execution metadata, payloads, and artifacts) is kept on the
server for a limited period, after which it is deleted automatically.

The period is not the same everywhere: each deployment sets its own default, and
it can be overridden for an individual account. Ask your system administrator
which period applies to you, or to have it changed.

tags.name: Iterations
tags.description:
An iteration reserves a quantum computer exclusively for the user, so that a
series of jobs can run one after another without waiting in the shared queue
between them. This suits iterative algorithms where each job depends on the
results of the previous one.

Create an iteration on the quantum computer, giving the longest duration
`max_duration_seconds` it may run. It joins the queue like a job, poll it until
its status turns `active`, which means the machine is now reserved dedicatedly.
Submit jobs to the iteration, and they run immediately, in the order you send
them. User can also submit jobs to the iteration while it is still in the queue,
and they will be executed once the iteration becomes active.

End the iteration as soon as your algorithm finishes, to release the quantum
computer reservation. Ending is refused while a job is still running on the
quantum computer, so a job already executing is never thrown away. Wait for the
running job to finish, or cancel that job first. Iteration also ends by itself
once the maximum duration elapses, or if no job is submitted within the idle
timeout. You are charged for the whole time the quantum computer was reserved,
whether it was running a job or not.

## When the reserved time runs out

Reaching `max_duration_seconds` does not stop a job in the middle of a run, and
it does not end the iteration on the spot. A job running on the quantum computer
is allowed to finish, and you are charged for that extra time as well. A job
that has not finished within a few minutes of the end is interrupted. The same
applies when the `idle_timeout_seconds` ends the iteration, though by then there
should not be any job running or waiting to be executed for the iteration.

- **Jobs still waiting in the iteration are cancelled** when it ends. They never
  started, so they cost nothing for the user. Submit them again outside the
  iteration, or in a new one, if you still want them run.
- **No further jobs are accepted** into the iteration once its time is up.
  Submitting one is rejected rather than queued, so nothing is left waiting in a
  reservation that is over.

tags.name: Calibration sets
tags.description:
The **Calibration Sets API** provides functionality for accessing quantum computer
calibrations and their associated data.

Calibrations are used internally to compile circuit-level jobs into pulse schedules.
Unless explicitly specified otherwise, the default calibration set is used during internal
operations. Official client libraries (e.g., `iqm-pulla`) use the same APIs to retrieve
calibrations for client-side pulse schedule generation.

Clients can programmatically load the contents and quality metrics (if available) of the
default calibration set. Calibration metrics for the current default calibration are also
visualized in the server’s web dashboard.

tags.name: Token management
tags.description:
Endpoints for refreshing and revocation of API tokens.

## Token limits

Each user has a limit on the number of simultaneously active API tokens per account.
The default limit is 10 unless your system administrator has changed it.
Attempts to create or activate a token beyond the limit will be rejected with a 403 error.
